records.why: KICD outcome (e) asks for the area of a regular heptagon and octagon, and the KICD learning experiences ask learners to use regular-polygon objects from their surroundings. Check: 360 ÷ 7 = 51.43°, half-angle 25.71°, tan 25.71° = 0.4816, apothem = 2 ÷ 0.4816 = 4.15 m, area = 7 × ½ × 4 × 4.15 = 58.1 m²; the formula (7/4)s² cot(180°/7) = 1.75 × 16 × 2.0765 = 58.14 m² agrees.

records.why: KICD outcome (c) and the KICD content list 'area of a triangle using Heron's formula', but it appeared nowhere. Lesson 6 is where triangles from a drawing are measured, so it is the natural place; the 40-minute Lesson 3 is already full. The shoelace formula is not KICD content, so it is now optional. Checked: 6, 8, 10 gives s = 12 and 12 × 6 × 4 × 2 = 576, √576 = 24 = ½ × 6 × 8. Triangle ACD of the pentagon A(0,0), C(5,2), D(4,5) has sides √29 = 5.385, √10 = 3.162, √41 = 6.403, s = 7.475, area √(7.475 × 2.090 × 4.313 × 1.072) = 8.50 cm², which equals the shoelace/triangulation value ½|5×5 − 4×2| = 8.5. Teacher decides whether to run it as a whole-class segment (suggested) or to move it elsewhere.
records.old: Extension segment (~10 minutes, flagged as 'Challenge for Fast Finishers and Future Surveyors'): Teacher introduces the coordinate/shoelace formula.
records.new: HERON'S FORMULA segment (~8 minutes, whole class): The teacher asks: 'What if a surveyor can measure only the three sides of a triangle and has no way to get the height?' Learners use s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2 and A = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)]. First check on a 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm triangle: s = 12, A = √(12 × 6 × 4 × 2) = √576 = 24 cm², the same as ½ × 6 × 8. Then learners measure the three sides of triangle ACD on their shamba diagram (about 5.4 cm, 3.2 cm and 6.4 cm), apply Heron's formula (about 8.5 cm², small differences come from rounding the measured sides) and compare with their ½bh answer for ACD. Extension segment (optional, for Fast Finishers and Future Surveyors; not KICD content): Teacher introduces the coordinate/shoelace formula.

records.value: (7 minutes) The teacher reads aloud the phenomenon narrative in brief: a community meeting in a village near Kericho; three farming families (the Chepkemoi family — tea, the Mwangi family — maize, and the Otieno family — mixed crops); the village elder's hand-drawn boundary; the community's disagreement about how to calculate the area. Learners follow along on their scaled drawings. The teacher displays an annotated diagram showing the seven boundary measurements (sides of 18 m, 22 m, 15 m, 20 m, 25 m, 17 m, 19 m) and the interior angles, pointing out that no two sides are equal and no angle is 90°. In groups of four, for 3 minutes, learners complete an 'Observation Record' in their books: (i) List every standard area formula you know (rectangle, square, triangle, circle, etc.). (ii) Put a tick next to any formula that could directly give you the area of this plot. (iii) Write one sentence: 'This plot is puzzling because ___.' Three or four groups read their sentence aloud (about 30 seconds each).

records.value: PART A — TRIANGLE AREA REVIEW (6 min): Each learner receives two pre-cut card triangles — one right-angled (base 8 cm, height 6 cm) and one acute (base 10 cm, height 5 cm). Learners measure the base and perpendicular height of each using a ruler, calculate the area using A = ½bh and record working in their books (3 minutes, individual). They compare answers with their partner. The teacher then demonstrates on the board, using the acute triangle, that the HEIGHT is the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex — NOT the slant side — and draws the altitude with a dashed red marker, labelling it h. Learners correct any errors. PART B — CONNECTING TO THE PHENOMENON (8 min): The teacher draws a simplified version of the Kericho heptagon on the board and asks: 'What if we drew lines from ONE vertex — say, peg A — to every other non-adjacent vertex? What shapes would we create?' After 1 minute of pair discussion, the teacher draws the diagonals from vertex A, creating five triangles. Learners count: 'A heptagon cut this way gives us FIVE triangles.' Each learner then marks the base and height of triangle A-B-C on their scaled drawing and checks with a partner. Learners record in their books: 'If I can find the area of each triangle, I can add them up to find the total area of the plot. This means the area of a triangle is the BUILDING BLOCK for finding the area of any polygon.'

(ii) For the rhombus — measure both diagonals. (iii) For the trapezium — measure both parallel sides (a and b) and the perpendicular height. (iv) For the kite — measure both diagonals. Groups that finish early draw a diagonal on the trapezium to split it into two triangles and label their bases and common height; the trapezium and kite derivations are completed in the Explain phase. records.value: (14 minutes) Using their Dimensions Table from Phase 2, groups derive the area formula for each quadrilateral and calculate the area of their specific cut-out (5 minutes). They record: 'The area of a parallelogram = __ because when we rearranged it we got a rectangle of base __ and height __.' Similarly for the rhombus (the diagonals cross at right angles and bisect each other, giving four congruent right-angled triangles with legs ½d₁ and ½d₂), trapezium (two triangles with bases a and b sharing height h), and kite (the diagonals cross at right angles; the diagonal d₂ splits the kite into two triangles with the same base d₂ whose heights add up to d₁, so A = ½d₂d₁). The teacher then formalises all four formulae on the board with derivation diagrams (4 minutes). Learners apply the formulae to two contextualised problems (5 minutes): (1) A parallelogram-shaped cattle pen near Naivasha has a base of 24 m and a perpendicular height of 15 m. What is its area? (2) A tea-farm terrace in Kericho has a trapezoidal cross-section with parallel widths of 3.6 m and 2.2 m and a depth of 1.4 m. What is the cross-sectional area? Learners finish with a short link to the Kericho plot.

records.value: (14 minutes) Groups of four receive: one large printed heptagon (scale 1 cm = 5 m), a set of 5 pre-cut blank triangular card cut-outs (labelled T1–T5), a 30 cm ruler, a sharp pencil, and a recording table (columns: Triangle | Base (cm) | Height (cm) | Area (cm²)). Step 1 (3 min): Groups agree on one interior vertex from which to draw all diagonals. They draw four diagonals, dividing the heptagon into exactly five triangles, and label them T1–T5. Step 2 (5 min): For each triangle, learners place the triangular card cut-out over it to confirm non-overlap and full coverage, then measure the base (any side) and the corresponding perpendicular height with the ruler, recording values to the nearest millimetre (members share the five triangles between them). Step 3 (3 min): Each group member calculates the area of their triangles using A = ½ × base × height, recording in cm². Step 4 (3 min): The group sums the five triangle areas to get the total heptagon area in cm², then applies the scale conversion (1 cm = 5 m, so 1 cm² = 25 m²) to find the real plot area in m². Learners record the final answer prominently on their poster sheet. Groups that finish early check one triangle a second way: measure two sides and the angle between them with the protractor, apply A = ½ab sin C from Lesson 3, and compare (the two answers should agree within about 5%).

records.value: (18 minutes) PART A — Decomposition Method (Groups, 4 min): Using their measured apothem from the scale diagram (apothem ≈ 3.62 m for side = 3 m; students derive this from their scale measurement), each group calculates: Area of one isosceles triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 3 × 3.62 ≈ 5.43 m². Total octagon area = 8 × 5.43 ≈ 43.5 m². Students record this in their worksheet. PART B — Formula Method (Teacher-led, 5 min): Teacher writes on the board: A = 2(1 + √2)s² and guides the class through the derivation step-by-step: 'Each isosceles triangle has base s and height (apothem) = s/2 × (1 + √2). (Split one triangle in half: the right-angled triangle has angle 22.5° and the side s/2 opposite it, so apothem = (s/2) ÷ tan 22.5°; since tan 22.5° = √2 − 1, 1 ÷ tan 22.5° = √2 + 1, and with s = 3 m this is 1.5 ÷ 0.4142 ≈ 3.62 m.) Area of 8 triangles = 8 × [½ × s × s/2 × (1 + √2)] = 2(1 + √2)s².' Students substitute s = 3 m: A = 2(1 + 1.414) × 9 = 2 × 2.414 × 9 = 43.45 m². PART C — Verification (1 min): Students compare their two answers and write a 2-sentence justification of why they are almost identical and which method they would trust. PART D — Tile and Cost Calculation (Groups, 4 min): Area of one tile = 0.25 × 0.25 = 0.0625 m². Number of tiles = 43.45 ÷ 0.0625 = 695.2 → round up to 696 tiles. Add 10% wastage (standard construction practice in Kenya): 696 × 1.10 = 766 tiles. Total cost = 766 × Ksh 85 = Ksh 65,110. Groups record and compare their cost estimates with their original predictions. PART E — Kericho Connection (1 min): One sentence to a partner on how the octagon decomposition helps with the Kericho seven-sided plot. PART F — Regular heptagon (3 min): A regular heptagon has side 4 m. Learners use the same decomposition from the centre (seven congruent isosceles triangles, central angle 360° ÷ 7 ≈ 51.4°) with the apothem 4.15 m (given, or found as 2 ÷ tan 25.7° ≈ 2 ÷ 0.4816) to find its area: 7 × ½ × 4 × 4.15 ≈ 58.1 m². Homework (outside lesson time): find one object or pattern at home or school shaped like a regular polygon (for example a hexagonal nut, an octagonal road sign or a hexagonal tile), measure its side, and estimate its area with the decomposition method.

records.new: (18 minutes) PART A — Decomposition Method (Groups, 4 min): Using their measured apothem from the scale diagram (apothem ≈ 3.62 m for side = 3 m; students derive this from their scale measurement), each group calculates: Area of one isosceles triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 3 × 3.62 ≈ 5.43 m². Total octagon area = 8 × 5.43 ≈ 43.5 m². Students record this in their worksheet. PART B — Formula Method (Teacher-led, 5 min): Teacher writes on the board: A = 2(1 + √2)s² and guides the class through the derivation step-by-step: 'Each isosceles triangle has base s and height (apothem) = s/2 × (1 + √2). (Split one triangle in half: the right-angled triangle has angle 22.5° and the side s/2 opposite it, so apothem = (s/2) ÷ tan 22.5°; since tan 22.5° = √2 − 1, 1 ÷ tan 22.5° = √2 + 1, and with s = 3 m this is 1.5 ÷ 0.4142 ≈ 3.62 m.) Area of 8 triangles = 8 × [½ × s × s/2 × (1 + √2)] = 2(1 + √2)s².' Students substitute s = 3 m: A = 2(1 + 1.414) × 9 = 2 × 2.414 × 9 = 43.45 m². PART C — Verification (1 min): Students compare their two answers and write a 2-sentence justification of why they are almost identical and which method they would trust. PART D — Tile and Cost Calculation (Groups, 4 min): Area of one tile = 0.25 × 0.25 = 0.0625 m². Number of tiles = 43.45 ÷ 0.0625 = 695.2 → round up to 696 tiles. Add 10% wastage (standard construction practice in Kenya): 696 × 1.10 = 766 tiles. Total cost = 766 × Ksh 85 = Ksh 65,110. Groups record and compare their cost estimates with their original predictions. PART E — Kericho Connection (1 min): One sentence to a partner on how the octagon decomposition helps with the Kericho seven-sided plot. The final 6-minute Model Building Phase has each learner revise their running cumulative model (started in Lesson 1) to incorporate the composite-polygon principle and add the Kericho solution, ready for the Lesson 8 presentation.

They write two predictions on a sticky note: (1) 'I think the plot is made up of ___ standard shapes,' and (2) 'My rough estimate of the total area is ___ m².' Predictions are posted on a class Predict Wall beside the Driving Question Board. records.value: (8 minutes) Groups post their completed evidence tables and worked solutions for both composite problems on the classroom walls (Gallery Walk setup). Each group's paper must include: the decomposition diagram (labelled), the evidence table, and the final area. Groups rotate in a set direction, spending 2 minutes at each of two other groups' posters (4 minutes). At each poster, they place a green sticky note if they agree with the solution and can confirm the arithmetic, or a yellow sticky note if they found an error or used a different decomposition that gave a different answer, writing the specific step where they diverged. Groups return to their own poster, read the feedback, and have 1 minute to defend their answer or correct an error. The whole class then converges for a 3-minute teacher-led synthesis: the teacher writes the generalised composite-polygon rule on the board — 'Total Area = Sum of component areas (addition) OR Whole area minus removed area (subtraction)' — and connects it explicitly to the Kericho plot: 'The Kericho plot is a composite polygon. The same rule you just applied to the school building and the community garden applies directly to the village elder's boundary.'

records.value: (12 minutes) Groups return to the scaled Kericho plot worksheet from Phase 1. Each group has 8 minutes to produce a justified solution to the anchoring phenomenon: (1) Decompose the seven-sided plot into standard shapes using internal construction lines, labelling every sub-shape with its name, dimensions, and calculated area. (2) Sum the component areas to find the total plot area in m². (3) Divide the total area by 3 to find the equal share for each of the three farming families (the Chepkemoi family for tea, the Mwangi family for maize, and the Otieno family for mixed crops). (4) On the same diagram, shade and label the three sections with each family's name and area. (5) Write one sentence justifying why the division is fair (equal area) and whether the shape of each section is practical for farming. At 8 minutes, each group nominates one spokesperson, who gives a 30-second summary of their group's total area and proposed division (3 minutes in all). The class votes with thumbs: up (agree with total area), sideways (unsure), down (disagree with total). Groups with thumbs-down neighbours must note the discrepancy for Lesson 8. The teacher then updates the class Driving Question Board (1 minute): moves the card 'Can any polygon be broken into shapes we know?' to the 'We Now Know' column, and adds a new card: 'Does the shape of each family's section affect its farming usefulness? (Lesson 8).'

records.value: (6 minutes) Each learner opens their individual running cumulative model — a diagrammatic record updated at the end of every lesson since Lesson 1 that shows how their understanding of polygon area has grown. In Lesson 1 it showed the triangle and decomposition idea; in Lessons 2–3 it grew to include the quadrilateral formulae and A = ½ab sin C; in Lessons 4–5 it grew to include heptagon and octagon decomposition; in Lesson 6 it incorporated irregular polygon triangulation and Heron's formula. Now, in 5 minutes, each learner adds a new section to their model titled 'Composite Polygons — Lesson 7.' In this section they must: (i) draw and label one example of an additive composite polygon (like the L-shaped building) and one example of a subtractive composite polygon (like the pentagonal garden); (ii) write the general rule: Area(composite) = Σ Area(components) ± Area(removed section); (iii) draw a small thumbnail of the Kericho plot with their chosen decomposition and write their group's total area. In the final minute, learners write one 'remaining question' on a sticky note and add it to the DQB. Examples the teacher anticipates: 'What if we can't measure the height of a triangle inside the plot?', 'Is there a single formula for any polygon?', 'What if the land is on a slope?'
